newsitem.title: TURKEY: U.S. envoy confident of calm in Cyprus row.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy confident of calm in Cyprus row.

text.p: U.S. envoy Carey Cavanaugh ended a trip to the eastern Mediterranean on Thursday confident he had put the lid on a potentially explosive row between Turkey and its Greek rivals over a missile purchase by Cyprus.

"This visit has turned out to be a successful diplomatic mission in what the United States was concerned could have been a crisis atmosphere," Cavanaugh told a news conference in the Turkish capital after stops in Cyprus and Athens.

Cavanaugh said a key to cooling tempers was a promise he had gained from Greek Cypriot officials that they would not go ahead with the planned installment of anti-aircraft missiles on the divided island for another 16 months.
Turkey threatened several times last week to use force in Cyprus to halt the deployment, raising the spectre of a wider conflict with fellow NATO member Greece.
"What we have been able to do is assure that there is a substantial period of time in which this issue can be addressed," he said.
But Turkey has discounted some of Cavanaugh's optimism. It says the 16-month timeframe is meaningless because the S-300 missiles were not due to be delivered from Russia until mid-1998 anyway.
Ankara has not backed down on its threats to strike and the Greek Cypriots insist they will still set up the missile system.
"For as long as it (Cyprus) keeps to this decision our stance will remain in effect in the same form and the same strength," a foreign ministry spokesman said on Wednesday.

Cyprus has been divided since Turkey invaded in 1974 in response to a Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military government then ruling Greece. Ankara maintains some 30,000 troops in a self-declared Turkish Cypriot state in the north.
Athens has a defence pact with the Greek Cypriot administration, regarded internationally as the island's only legitimate government.
Cavanaugh said he had told Turkey of U.S. opposition to its threats to use force in Cyprus again. "We were firm in our view that there was no acceptable aggressive response."
Washington will continue to oppose the Cypriot missile deal.
"(The Greek Cypriots) understand that will remain the position of the United States government. These missiles should never come to that island," he said.
Cyprus said on Wednesday the missile system would cost an estimated 200 million Cyprus pounds ($426 million).
The semi-official Cyprus News Agency quoted Yiannakis Cassoulides, Cypriot government spokesman, as saying there was no clause allowing the government to cancel the deal.
Cavanaugh dismissed Turkish fears that Ankara may be asked to cut its troop level in north Cyprus in return for the missile deployment being scrapped.

"I don't expect Turkey to have to bargain to get the deal reversed. The hope is that the United States and others in the international community will be able to do that to make it clear the missiles aren't needed," he said.
Western diplomats in Turkey say the United States will now use the 16 months to pressure Cyprus not to buy the missiles or persuade Moscow not to sell them.

Earlier this week, the rival communities in Cyprus were united only in refuting State Department comments suggesting they had agreed to implement confidence building measures on the U.N. "Green Line" dividing the island.
Four Greek Cypriot civilians and a Turkish Cypriot soldier have died along the line in recent months in the worst political violence since 1974.
